Federal Reserve Board · 16–20 November 2026

Did Fed speakers signal a rate move?

Two speakers favoured further tightening. One described conditions that could pull policy in either direction. Four speeches gave no current rate guidance.

How to read a score

Read each speaker’s stated preference for the current or prospective US policy rate. The unit is one set of prepared remarks. A speaker can discuss inflation, payments or financial risks without taking a position on rates.

On this editorial scale, +2 and −2 denote an advocated tightening or easing, respectively. +1 and −1 denote a directional lean conditional on the speaker’s baseline. Zero is reserved for an explicit preference to maintain the current rate. Two-sided conditions without a preferred direction and speeches without guidance both receive a blank numeric score.

These seven readings use the official speech texts available through 20 November. The scores describe individuals’ views. Market expectations, changes from a previous speech and the size of any likely rate move require separate evidence.

The same December fed funds futures contract (ZQZ6) trades throughout the week. Its final settlement at 3 p.m. ET implies a change from the 3.88% effective rate assuming one move effective 10 December. Daily changes use unrounded inputs and include other news. Speakers on the same day share one pair of settlements.

Seven speeches

Lisa D. Cook · 20 November

+2 · Hawkish · supports further tightening

Cook judged financial conditions too accommodative and said waiting carried inflation risks. She had preferred another quarter-point increase in October. The size and number of future moves still depended on the data.

“I am skeptical that September's single 1/4 point rate increase will be enough to change the path of inflation.”

Philip N. Jefferson · 19 November

Two-sided conditions · no preferred direction

Jefferson would respond more strongly to inflation if expectations risked becoming unanchored. Contained price pressure would give more weight to employment. He did not choose between the scenarios or advocate holding rates.

“If price pressures are contained, it may be prudent to prioritize downside risks to employment.”

Michael S. Barr · 18 November

+1 · Hawkish lean · conditional on his forecast

In a speech mainly about community investment, Barr included a personal policy outlook. His forecast points to further increases, with timing and size left open.

“If the economy evolves as I currently forecast, I expect it will be appropriate to raise rates further”

Christopher J. Waller · 17 November

No rate guidance · payment systems

Waller discussed how settlement infrastructure and tokenization could affect payments. He did not give a current preference for the federal funds rate.

“The Federal Reserve can support these solutions by providing core payment and settlement infrastructure upon which the private sector can innovate”

Kevin Warsh · 16 November

No rate guidance · productivity research

Warsh described possible productivity and employment outcomes and their longer-run implications for monetary policy. The remarks did not specify a preferred current rate path.

“Will this new technology deliver a rise in total factor productivity?”

Michael S. Barr · 16 November

No rate guidance · financial stability

Barr examined leverage in data centers and vulnerabilities linked to AI adoption. The risks he discussed concern financial stability and carry no explicit recommendation for the policy rate.

“In addition to the question of equity valuations, the AI buildout has been increasingly funded by debt.”
